extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates learning algebraic geometry (schemes, functors, morphisms); researchers needing foundations
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, properties, and exercises for representable functors, group objects (group schemes), and many useful classes of morphisms of schemes (open embeddings, affine, quasicompact, quasiseparated, finite/integral, etc.), together with key lemmas (Qcqs Lemma, Nakayama) and geometric translations of algebraic theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representable functor / represented by Y
rubrics_metrics.description: A contravariant functor F : C → Sets is represented by Y if it is naturally isomorphic to the functor h_Y (h_Y(X) = Mor(X, Y)). We say F is representable if it is represented by some Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bijection in examples (e.g., Mor(X,A^1) ≅ Γ(X,O_X)) is an instance of representability; naturality means the bijection is a natural isomorphism of functors (functoriality in X). Exercises show examples: A^n represents the functor of n functions (Γ(X,O_X)^n), Spec Z[t,t^{-1}] represents invertible functions (G_m).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of representing object up to unique isomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: If a contravariant functor F is represented by Y and by Z, then there is a unique isomorphism Y ≅ Z induced by the natural isomorphism of functors h_Y ≅ h_Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a universal-property style uniqueness statement (see Exercise 6.6.C); hint: it's the usual 'unique up to unique isomorphism' consequence of universal properties and extends to Yoneda's Lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group object / group scheme axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: A group object in a category C (assumed to have a final object Z and products) is an object X together with morphisms multiplication m: X×X → X, inverse i: X → X, and identity e: Z → X satisfying associativity, identity, and inverse axioms expressed by commutative diagrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit axioms: (i) associativity: (m,id)∘m = (id,m)∘m on X×X×X; (ii) identity diagrams showing e acts as identity; (iii) inverse diagrams showing composition with inverse gives identity (see text diagrams). Specialization to Sets recovers ordinary groups. Group scheme = group object in category of schemes (or in A-schemes or S-schemes for base). Exercises: give A^1_Z the group-scheme structure, compute maps for GL_n, det, kernels, µ_n, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable class of morphisms — three desiderata
rubrics_metrics.description: Any 'reasonable' class of morphisms should satisfy: (i) local on the target, (ii) closed under composition, and (iii) closed under base change (pullback / fibered product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local on the target means checking the property can be done after restricting to open covers of the target; composition closure and base-change closure are essential for stability of the class. The text emphasizes asking these three questions for any new class of morphisms. Examples/verification exercises are provided for open embeddings and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open embedding (open immersion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An open embedding of schemes is a morphism π : (X,O_X) → (Y,O_Y) that factors as an isomorphism to an open subscheme (U, O_Y|_U) followed by the inclusion into Y. Equivalently, π is a bijection onto an open subset with the scheme structure pulled back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequences: isomorphisms are open embeddings; notation often uses a symbol (e.g., '↪' or similar). Distinguish open subscheme (subset inclusion) versus open embedding (isomorphism onto an open). Exercises verify the three desiderata for open embeddings: local on target, closed under composition, and closed under base change. Exercise notes: open embeddings need not be local on the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasicompact morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is quasicompact if for every affine open subset U of Y, the preimage π^{-1}(U) is quasicompact (equivalently, preimage of any quasi-compact open is quasi-compact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard notion to control 'finiteness' of the topology of fibers; composition of quasicompact morphisms is quasicompact (exercise). Quasicompactness is affine-local on the target (check on an affine cover). Many 'reasonable' schemes/morphisms coming from Noetherian sources are quasicompact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiseparated morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is quasiseparated if for every affine open subset U of Y, the preimage π^{-1}(U) is a quasiseparated scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used often together with quasicompactness (abbreviated 'qcqs'). Many common morphisms (from locally Noetherian schemes, affine morphisms, separated morphisms) are quasiseparated. Quasiseparatedness is affine-local on the target (exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is affine if for every affine open set U of Y, the preimage π^{-1}(U) is an affine scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affine morphisms are quasicompact and quasiseparated. Affineness is affine-local on the target: it suffices to check on a cover of Y by affine opens U with π^{-1}(U) affine. Composition of affine morphisms is affine. The proof that 'affine' is affine-local on the target is nontrivial and is treated in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affineness is affine-local on the target (property)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is affine if there exists a cover of Y by affine open sets U such that each π^{-1}(U) is affine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a proposition and noted as the hardest part of the section; a lemma and further machinery are used in its proof. Useful for checking affineness by local testing on target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qcqs Lemma (sections and localization)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a quasicompact quasiseparated scheme and s ∈ Γ(X,O_X), then the natural map Γ(X,O_X)_s → Γ(X_s,O_X) is an isomorphism, where X_s is the locus where s does not vanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoids affine-specific notation D(s) to emphasize generality; the lemma generalizes the affine case (where it's immediate). Exercise asks to identify the natural map via universal property of localization. Useful technical tool when working with qcqs schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning properties of schemes into properties of morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is a property of schemes, one often says a morphism π : X → Y 'has P' if for every affine open U ⊂ Y the preimage π^{-1}(U) has property P (with suitable hypotheses like Affine Communication Lemma allowing checks on affine covers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This viewpoint (Grothendieck's philosophy) lets one treat properties as relative; examples include quasicompact, quasiseparated, affine, etc. Informally think of π having P as 'all fibers have P' but actually requires good behavior as fibers vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral ring homomorphism / integral extension
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring homomorphism φ : B → A is integral if every element of A satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in φ(B). An integral extension is an integral homomorphism that is also an inclusion of rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent characterization (Lemma 7.2.1): a ∈ A is integral over B iff a is contained in a subalgebra of A that is a finitely generated B-module. Corollary: finite (i.e., A a finitely generated B-module) implies integral; converse false in general. Exercises describe preservation properties under localization and quotients and give counterexamples (e.g., k[t] → k[t](t)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lying Over Theorem (integral extensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ : B → A is an integral extension, then for any prime ideal q ⊂ B there exists a prime ideal p ⊂ A with p ∩ B = q; equivalently, the map Spec A → Spec B is (set-theoretically) surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric translation: above every 'downstairs' prime there is a prime 'upstairs' (p lies over q). Proof sketch uses localization and reduction to maximal ideals and Exercise 7.2.E; figure provided in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Going-Up Theorem (integral homomorphism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose φ : B → A is integral. Given chains of prime ideals q1 ⊂ ... ⊂ qn in B and p1 ⊂ ... ⊂ pm in A such that each p_i lies over q_i (and m < n), then the chain p1 ⊂ ... ⊂ pm can be extended to p1 ⊂ ... ⊂ pn with each p_j lying over q_j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an extension property of prime chains under integral homomorphisms; text suggests reducing to simpler cases and drawing a picture. (Going-Down analogues require different hypotheses.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nakayama's Lemma (multiple versions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several related statements: Version 1 — if A ring, I ideal, M finitely generated A-module with M = I M, then there exists a ∈ 1+I with a M = 0 (equivalently some i ≡ 1 (mod I) annihilates M). Version 2 — if I is contained in all maximal ideals (e.g., maximal ideal in local ring) and M finitely generated with M = I M then M = 0. Other versions: lifting generators from M/mM to M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the adjugate/matrix trick from Lemma 7.2.1. Exercises include important corollaries: generators of M/mM lift to generators of M in local rings, and other formulations useful for geometric interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability of kernels and functor-to-group-scheme correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: If F : G1 → G2 is a morphism of group schemes, consider the contravariant functor X ↦ ker(Mor(X,G1) → Mor(X,G2)); if this functor is representable, its representing object is the kernel of F in the category of group schemes. More generally, a contravariant functor Sch → Groups whose underlying functor to Sets is representable by Y determines unique structure maps m,i,e on Y making it a group scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 6.6.K and 6.6.O show how group operations on F(X) force the structure of a group scheme on the representing object Y. Applications: SL_n as kernel of det: GL_n → G_m, µ_n as kernel of (·)^n on G_m, etc.
